html:
The Porticus Aemilia was a huge warehouse in Rome, built in 193 BCE beside the city's river port on the Tiber. It was one of the largest commercial buildings of its time, almost half a kilometre long.

Rome was growing fast after the Second Punic War, and it fed itself more and more with goods shipped in from overseas: grain, wine, olive oil and building materials. Ships came up the Tiber to the new port district, the Emporium, below the Aventine hill. The Porticus Aemilia stored the cargoes and sent them out across the city. It was built by two officials from the Aemilius family, one of them Lucius Aemilius Paullus, who later conquered Macedon, and rebuilt in 174 BCE.

It is one of the earliest big buildings made with Roman concrete, with rows of vaulted halls. Some scholars now argue that the ruins usually given this name were really sheds for warships. The district around it became the warehouse quarter of Rome, and nearby rose Monte Testaccio, a hill made of broken oil jars from the oil trade. Later the grain dole depended on this kind of storage.
sum: The Porticus Aemilia was a huge warehouse in Rome, built in 193 BCE beside the city's river port on the Tiber. It was one of the largest commercial buildings of its time, almost half a kilometre long.
